extracted.intended_audience: students of mathematical logic (advanced undergraduates / beginning graduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of syntax and semantics of first-order logic and computability/decidability notions: definitions (terms, atomic formulas, wffs, free variables, sentences, structures), key theorems about effective enumerability/decidability, and the satisfaction relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semidecidable (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A of expressions is semidecidable iff there exists an effective procedure that, given any expression ε, produces the answer “yes” iff ε ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ε ∉ A no answer is ever given; this asymmetry is what prevents semidecidability alone from yielding decidability. (Original wording: "A set A of expressions is semidecidable iff there exists an effective procedure that, given any expression ε, produces the answer 'yes' iff ε ∈ A.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectively enumerable iff semidecidable (Theorem 17E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 17E: a set is effectively enumerable iff it is semidecidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea / constructive schemes are given: (1) from an effective enumeration you can semidecide membership by watching the enumeration and answering 'yes' when ε appears; (2) conversely, given a semidecision procedure, enumerate all expressions ε1, ε2, ... and dovetail (spend 1 minute on ε1, then 2 minutes on ε1 and ε2, then 3 minutes on ε1,ε2,ε3, ...) running the semidecision procedure in parallel so that every member of A will eventually be 'yes' and thus listed. Note: duplicates may appear unless checked for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidable implies semidecidable / effectively enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Any decidable set is also semidecidable, and hence any decidable set is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: a decider gives both 'yes' and 'no' answers; if the 'no' answer is ignored (or the 'no' bulb burned out) one still has a semidecision procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidable iff both it and its complement effectively enumerable (Theorem 17F / Kleene's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of expressions is decidable iff both it and its complement (relative to the set of all expressions) are effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark (exercise): 'Two semidecision procedures make a whole.' This reflects the constructive idea: run semideciders for A and for its complement in dovetailed fashion until one outputs 'yes'. (Original name: "Kleene's theorem.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of effective enumerability under union and intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: If sets A and B are effectively enumerable, then so are A ∪ B and A ∩ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Exercise 11; dovetailing / pairing enumerations give constructive enumerations for unions and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties of decidable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The class of decidable sets is closed under union, intersection, and complementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from decidability and classical boolean operations on characteristic deciders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautological consequences of an effectively enumerable/decidable set (Theorem 17G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ is a decidable (or effectively enumerable) set of wffs, then the set of tautological consequences of Σ is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: enumerate Σ as σ1,σ2,... and for any candidate τ test (by truth tables) whether ∅ |= τ, {σ1} |= τ, {σ1,σ2} |= τ, ...; use the corollary to the compactness theorem to ensure that if Σ |= τ some finite subset will witness it, so the procedure eventually answers 'yes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective computability of functions (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is effectively computable (computable) iff there exists an effective procedure that, given an input x, will eventually produce the correct output f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parallels semidecidability/enumerability notions but for functions rather than sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of effective enumerability via decidable set of pairs (Exercise 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A of expressions is effectively enumerable iff there is a decidable set B of pairs (α,n) (expression α and integer n) such that A = dom(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an alternative representation of enumerability in terms of decidable relations on pairs (useful for coding and reductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms (formation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms are expressions built up from constant symbols and variables by applying zero or more times the term-building operations F_f for each n-place function symbol f (Polish notation: f t1...tn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no function symbols, terms are just constants and variables. Unique readability of terms is asserted (proved in Section 2.3). Examples: + v2 S0, SSSS0, + E v1 SS0 E v2 SS0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic formulas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atomic formulas are expressions of the form P t1 ... tn where P is an n-place predicate symbol and t1,...,tn are terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atomic formulas play the role analogous to sentence symbols in sentential logic; examples include = v1 v2 and ∈ v5 v3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formulas (wffs) (formation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wffs are expressions built up from atomic formulas by applying (zero or more times) the formula-building operations E¬(γ) = (¬ γ), E→(γ,δ) = (γ → δ), and Qi(γ) = ∀ vi γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The set of wffs is defined inductively; arbitrary expressions need not be wffs. Unique decomposition of wffs is referenced as proven later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free variable (recursive definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of 'x occurs free in α' given recursively: (1) for atomic α, x occurs free iff x occurs in α; (2) x occurs free in ¬α iff x occurs free in α; (3) x occurs free in (α → β) iff it occurs free in α or β; (4) x occurs free in ∀ vi α iff x occurs free in α and x ≠ vi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is restated as a function h assigning to each wff the set of free variables; existence and uniqueness of h follow from the recursion theorem and unique decomposition of wffs. Examples distinguish sentences from non-sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is a wff in which no variable occurs free (i.e., h(α) = ∅).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences are the wffs translatable into English without blanks; other wffs serve as building blocks. Examples: ∀ v2(Av2 → Bv2) is a sentence; v1 occurs free in (∀ v1 Av1 → Bv1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational conventions and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted conventions: use only ¬ and → as primitive connectives; represent ∃ x α as ¬ ∀ x ¬ α; use Polish notation for function symbols; abbreviate (α ∨ β), (α ∧ β), (α ↔ β) in terms of ¬ and →; allow dropping outermost parentheses; binding strength rules (¬, ∀, ∃ apply to as little as possible); right-association of repeated →.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and warnings provided (e.g., differences between ∀ v(Av ∧ Bv) and ∀ v Av ∧ Bv, and how ∃ v(A v → B v) can be a much weaker claim than ∃ v(Av ∧ Bv)). Use conventions to increase readability but revert to primitive notation when exact symbol sequence matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique readability / recursion theorem dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique readability of terms and wffs is asserted (proved in Section 2.3) and is used to justify recursive definitions such as the free-variable function h and the extension of variable assignments to terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recursion theorem (Section 1.4) guarantees existence and uniqueness of such recursive definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure / model (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A for a first-order language assigns: (1) to the quantifier symbol ∀ a nonempty set |A| (the universe); (2) to each n-place predicate symbol P an n-ary relation P^A ⊆ |A|^n; (3) to each constant symbol c an element c^A ∈ |A|; (4) to each n-place function symbol f an n-ary operation f^A : |A|^n → |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universe must be nonempty; function symbols denote total functions on the universe; equality (if present) is a logical symbol and interpreted as actual equality in the domain. Examples: interpretations where ∈ is read as < on natural numbers, or finite structures pictured as directed graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction relation (|=_A φ[s]) — formal definition sketch
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction is defined for a structure A, a variable assignment s: V → |A|, and a wff φ: first extend s to terms by recursion (s(t) defined on variables, constants, and f t1...tn via f^A), then define satisfaction for atomic formulas (|=_A = t1 t2[s] iff s(t1)=s(t2); |=_A P t1...tn[s] iff (s(t1),...,s(tn)) ∈ P^A), and finally recursively for compound formulas and quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a mathematical definition of 'φ is true in A under assignment s' without appealing to informal English translations. For sentences, satisfaction does not depend on s; write |=_A σ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation patterns between English and formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical translation templates: 'Everything in category has property' → ∀ v( Category(v) → Property(v) ); 'There exists an object in category with property' → ∃ v( Category(v) ∧ Property(v) ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples (set-theory pair-set axiom, arithmetic statements, natural-language examples) show multi-step translation (introduce quantifiers, switch ∃ to ¬∀¬, put predicate/function symbols in left-most convention). Warnings about ambiguity in English and the need for multiple formalizations when English is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compactness and completeness in effective enumerability arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Compactness (and corollaries) is used as a tool: e.g., to show that if Σ |= τ then some finite subset of Σ entails τ, which justifies searching finite subsets to semidecide entailment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears explicitly in proof of Theorem 17G and in exercises 1–3 and 5–7; related to later completeness theorem statements (Exercise 7: existence of deduction from Σ when Σ |= τ).
